# dsh-agent-speedup

Tool-execution efficiency suite for DeepSeek Harness:
read-only result caching, speculative prefetch

, and concurrent readonly shell commands — each with a
measured, bounded scope.
## The honest premise

In our measurements across 6 real agent sessions (2,517 tool calls, 1,311 minutes), model latency
(T

TFT + thinking + generation) takes **87.2%** of the critical path, tool execution **22.1%**. This
pl

ugin works inside that 22% — nothing here reduces the number of model round trips, which is where
th

that 22% — nothing here reduces the number of model round trips, which is where
the other 78% lives.
Within that 22%, three different problems exist, and each capability targets one:
| Capability | Problem it solves | Measured |

| **Cache** | Same read-only call repeated | repeated read **2023 ms → 7 ms** (serial runs) |
| **In
-flight merge** | The same call repeated inside one parallel batch | 3 simultaneous reads span **202

7 ms total**, not 6 s |
| **Prefetch** | Files the model will ask for right after a `glob` | tool ti

me **10.08 s → 2.07 s (−79.4%)**; per-read median **2016 ms → 11 ms** |
| **Shell concurrency** | Mu
ltiple readonly shell commands serialized | window **13.81 s → 4.65 s (−66.3%)**, 4/4 commands in on
adonly shell commands serialized | window **13.81 s → 4.65 s (−66.3%)**, 4/4 commands in one batch |
Caching and scheduling are measured separately, on purpose. The concurrency figure above comes from

a
run with `cache: false, speculate: false` — nothing but scheduling is changed. Full method, paired
confidence intervals and the metric caveats: docs/BENCHMARK.md.

Both effects replicate on a stronger model (`deepseek-v4.1-flash`): prefetch/cache **−79.0%** tool
t

ime with a 70% hit rate, scheduling **−66.9%** tool window. Same direction, same magnitude — the
gai
n tracks the plugin, not the model.

And two things it deliberately does not fix: on local millisecond-scale tools the plugin is
invisibl

e (tools were 0.1–9.4% of wall in our runs), and DeepSeek Harness already parallel-batches
concurren

cy-safe tools — in our baseline 7 tool calls (6 reads + 1 shell) were dispatched within
19 ms with n
o plugin installed, and 5 adjacent tool results landed within 100 ms of each other.

**Different layer from HarnessMM.** HarnessMM also targets
DeepSeek Harness, but it removes *model r

easoning calls* by replaying guarded decisions; this plugin
removes *tool executions* and never touc

hes reasoning. They compose — a decision graph still names

The bundled `cordis.patch.yml` activates caching and prefetch immediately. Shell concurrency is
**of
f by default** — see the safety note below.
### Overriding config: replace, don't merge

A dsh patch entry with the same `id` **replaces the whole config object** — it does not merge. If
yo

u override one key, you must repeat every key you care about (the zod defaults fill in the rest,
but

your intent may differ from the defaults). The bundled defaults are in
cordis.patch.yml.
## The three capabilities
### Cache

Read-only tools (`read`, `glob`, `grep`, `read_image`, extendable) are cached by tool name plus
norm

alized arguments. On a hit the plugin returns the stored result without calling `next()` — the
real
dispatch never happens.

Entries carry a stat fingerprint (`size` + `mtimeMs`) checked on every hit, so a file changed by
any

means invalidates — including `bash`/`pwsh` writes, which emit no filesystem events.
`fs/write-inte
nt` and `fs/edit-intent` add immediate invalidation for the editor path.

Relative paths resolve against the **agent's session working directory**, the same base dsh's own
`r

ead` uses, so an agent that `cd`s elsewhere cannot collide with a same-named file elsewhere.
The cac

he is an LRU bounded by `maxEntries` (default 512), and a result whose file changed *during*
the rea

nded by `maxEntries` (default 512), and a result whose file changed *during*
the read is not stored.

**In-flight coalescing.** dsh dispatches a turn's read-only calls in one parallel batch. A batch
con

taining the same call twice would miss the cache both times, because neither has finished. Calls
tha

t arrive while an identical call is still running share that execution instead of repeating it —
thi
s covers the parallel case the cache alone cannot.

Tool names are matched literally. `read`, `glob`, `grep` and `read_image` are built in; any custom
o

r MCP tool you want cached must be listed in `readonlyTools` (and in `speculateOn` if its results
sh
ould trigger prefetch). Unknown names are never assumed safe.
### Prefetch

When a `glob` result comes back, the plugin pre-executes the same-family read tool for the first N
p

aths, in the background. Those results land in the same cache, so when the model actually asks,
noth

ing runs. Prefetch calls go through the ordinary pipeline — same agent context, same working
directo
ry, same guards — so denials and errors are handled identically.
### Shell concurrency
dsh's `bash` and `pwsh` tools declare no `isConcurrencySafe`, so every shell call runs exclusively —

four readonly `Get-*` calls that should share one parallel window instead took 7.1 s
(measured: per

-call gaps of 2.2–2.5 s). With this capability enabled, the same four calls completed
in 317 ms. The

capability attaches a conservative classifier that marks a command
concurrency-safe only when every
segment matches a readonly whitelist and no write pattern appears.

**This is off by default.** A classifier mistake means two shell commands with side effects run at
t
he same time. Enable it only if you accept that risk:
[代码示例省略，未执行]
The classifier is deliberately strict: `npm test`, `cargo build`, `python script.py` are all treated

as side-effecting (they may write), and unknown commands are rejected rather than guessed.
Subcomma

nds are handled per verb, not per program name — `git branch` (list) is readonly while
`git branch n

ew` (create) is not; `git remote` lists but `git remote add` rewrites config; `find`
